title: Firefighter challenges super fund benefit 'error'
full_text:
The nearly $40 billion pension plan for Victorian emergency service workers is under pressure to answer complaints from members who allege it has botched the calculation of their retirement benefits, potentially costing them hundreds of thousands of dollars when they exit the workforce.
Firefighter Grant Williams, 33, has taken Emergency Services and State Super, known as ESSSuper, to the state's civil and administrative tribunal to get the fund to open up its systems to outside scrutiny, alleging that there are "widespread inaccuracies" in its data and member benefit calculations.
Williams met with former chief executive Robbie Campo - now the CEO of industry fund giant HESTA - as well as executives Duncan Winton and Stuart Wilkinson last December to discuss the issue, but says his access to key data and information was shut down after the fact.
"We are not being afforded any transparency," he said. "The fund essentially has a monopoly over our retirement savings in that they don't have to compete for them, and it has affected the autonomy of emergency workers."
While most superannuation accounts rely on contributions from members and their employers for their balances, government-employed emergency services workers in Victoria operate on a defined benefit scheme.
These schemes are generally closed to the public at large and guarantee a predetermined pension based on a member's years of service and salary. They are largely based on programs that preceded the introduction of the superannuation guarantee in 1992, and their defined benefit entitlements cannot be transferred between funds.
Williams claims ESSSuper has severely underestimated the entitlement for him and a handful of others after they checked their annual statements and applied the benefit formula.
"I did some quick maths in my head, and it seemed far too low. We don't get transaction history or account statements [like a normal super fund with regular contributions], so I decided to call the fund and was told the balance was just my salary multiplied by the benefit calculation," he said.
"I can assure you that the number was not multiple times my salary."
It marks a second set of complaints about inaccurate benefit calculations at ESSSuper, which is already battling claims in the Victorian Supreme Court that it cost transport workers more than $40 million by not accounting for penalty shift allowances when determining their final pension payout.
ESSSuper is defending those claims, which were first brought by Gordon Legal in 2024. Williams said he planned to raise the issues at ESSSuper's annual member meeting, which is usually held in November but could be delayed until after the Victorian state election that same month.
"One of our big concerns is not being able to keep track of the benefit - it's about keeping up with the community standard and making sure we have the buying power that is the same as every other Australian," he said.
ESSSuper confirmed it had received nine complaints from five members about the operation of the defined benefit scheme, but said it would be inappropriate to discuss those matters publicly.
"ESSSuper is confident that defined benefit calculations are administered in accordance with governing rules and legislation," a spokesman said.
"The fund has established systems, processes and governance controls to administer defined benefit entitlements and calculate member benefits in accordance with the governing legislation and actuarial requirement."
ESSSuper said it was reliant on information from employers to determine the entitlements.
"Where data issues are identified, we work closely with the relevant employer to investigate, validate and, where required, correct records, so member benefits are calculated using accurate information.
"Our focus is on providing members with information they can rely on, rather than estimates based on information that may subsequently change."
